chapter_theme: The second half of Perunkadunko's paalaikkali (19 to 36): seven poems in which the woman or her friend argues against the man's leaving for wealth (his false promises, wealth moving by former deeds, love as a loan repaid with another face, the deer and elephant that keep together on the waste), then eleven spring poems in which the season's flowers, bees and cuckoos torment the woman left at home in Madurai by the Vaigai, most ending with the friend announcing that the man has come back on the promised day; the similes are drawn heavily from kingship, friendship and virtue.

19.reading: The woman tells the man that she could not have known his sweet words and gentle embrace were false; now that gossip the wide town cannot hold has come and she knows he means to cross the waste that even daylight shuns, he is no true man; let him go and finish his work, but let him not, his love gone, ask those who come from her how she whom he left is faring, for if he asks, his name bright as daylight may be marred and grief may overtake him there with the work undone.
19.nuance: The close is a blessing turned inside out: she protects his success by asking him to forget her, so that the grief of remembering would fall on him and his work, not on her. மகன் அல்லை ('you are no man') refuses him the name of a man of worth in one half-line.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's planned crossing of the waste for his work

comparisons.tenor: his good name, bright as daylight

20.reading: The woman answers the man who warns her off the waste where the sun's rage has dried the land, elephants languish, the hill burns and the pools are dust: to his 'can your feet bear a forest that never knew rain?' she says the days of life stay less than wind and she has his chest as her grace, so why perish in grief; to his 'there is no water on the road' she says youth runs off like river water and she has his heart for clear water, so why stay here bewildered; to his 'there are no shady trees there' she says she knows her colour will fade like shaded leaves, so why leave the shade of his feet; and to his 'the forest is too hot to approach' she asks whether he will not see, on the rocky track where no arrow passes, the doe following the handsome stag, and whether they part.
20.nuance: Each of his warnings flatters a part of her (parrot speech, nectar mouth, bamboo shoulders) and each answer turns it: her life is shorter than wind, her youth flows away like the river, her colour already fades; the poem ends not with argument but with the deer pair he will meet on the very road, which she makes his own witness against going alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaving for the waste and the woman refusing to stay behind

comparisons.tenor: the water of her mouth, sweet as nectar
her shoulders, which outdo the bamboo
the days of life, less steady than wind
her colour fading like tender leaves
his heart as the clear water she would drink

iraicchi.act: the doe follows the stag across the rocky waste and the pair do not part
iraicchi.sense: if even the deer cross the waste together, the wife should not be left behind by her husband

21.reading: The friend tells the man that he has spoken two things, the graceless word that he must leave for wealth to the far land where a lone tusker, cut off from its herd, with milk-white tusks and mortar-like feet, guards the road, and the kind word, stroking her brow, that he will not leave her and she must not fear; which of them is true, she asks, when wealth does not stay with those who call themselves its owners but moves from one to another by former deeds; for such wealth he leaves, and without him the girl will not live the space of a blink, forgetting the beauty of her shoulders.
21.nuance: The friend turns the man's reason against him: if wealth comes and goes by பழ வினை, no journey can earn it, while the girl's life cannot be had again. The lone tusker that has left its herd (இனம் பிரி ஒருத்தல்) is a near miss for iraicchi: it mirrors the man who leaves his own, but it stands inside his own description of the road and does nothing a person of the situation does beyond being alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's announced departure for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the tusker's tusks, white as milk

22.reading: The woman tells the man that a borrower's face when he asks and when he repays differ, as the world has always known; women of beauty go where their lovers' word leads them, like dolls a mother has given life to, and once their beauty has been sipped as a bee sips pollen, what is this wealth strangers talk of? He praised her teeth set like jasmine buds, her hair glowing like gems through oil, her breasts like the green lotus buds of the pond; did he ever praise the teeth falling, the hair's later care, the slack breasts? And as he goes to the sun-scorched waste while the gold-bright lines of her skin fade, she asks whether they ever stood before him telling their grief when want pressed hard.
22.nuance: The opening proverb makes love a loan: he borrowed her youth with one face and will repay it with another. Each praise is answered by the same part grown old, so his catalogue of beauty becomes a contract for her whole life. The closing question seems to say they never complained to him of poverty, so his journey answers a need they never voiced; lines 5 to 8 and 19 to 22 are hard and this reading is not settled.

thinai_evidence.note: the man going to the scorched waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the lover, pleading while he takes her beauty and another man once it is spent
women of beauty, moved by their lovers' word
his enjoyment of her beauty, as a bee sips pollen

comparisons.vehicle: நெய் இடை நீவி மணி ஒளி விட்டன்ன

comparisons.tenor: the lovely lines on her skin

23.reading: The woman tells the man that for him to cross alone the burnt waste of blocking hills, where elephant-scarers' slings knock the flowers from the boughs, while she stays behind, would make her a mockery to this gossiping town; she will neither eat nor live, for women whose beauty is enjoyed and then abandoned are like a leaf cup once its water is drunk, like a town its dwellers have left, like a flower thrown away once worn, and she is such in his heart; so let him keep her heart, which runs to him like a young doe that, hunted by killing dogs, takes refuge with the netters, and not send it back to her.
23.nuance: The doe that flees the dogs into the hunters' nets is the poem's sharpest figure: her heart goes for safety to the very man whose leaving hurts her, and she asks him to keep it rather than return it. குடை in line 9 seems to be a leaf cup thrown away after drinking; வேள் நீர் is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: he crosses the waste alone and she is left behind

comparisons.tenor: women whose virtue was enjoyed and then cast off
her heart, running for refuge to the one who will hurt it

24.reading: The woman tells her friend that the saying 'what one fears, hearing it and suspecting it with a trembling heart, becomes the very affliction' is true: when her man kept praising her as if she were new, she sensed something and, to find it out, lay with him on the clean wide bed; asleep and dreaming of her shoulders he said, 'Will she of the bangled wrists bear it without breaking and guard the house while I cross the long-hilled waste, where tusked elephants run to the mirage, and stay until the wealth is won?'; if that is his mind, since she has no strength to live without him, and lest small people blame him as the man who left her, her life has gone with him: let the friend tell him so.
24.nuance: The departure is learned from sleep-talk: he says in a dream what he will not say awake, and the proverb that opens the poem (அஞ்சியது ஆங்கே அணங்கு ஆகும்) frames it as a fear made real by being looked into. Her life leaving with him is offered to save his name, not hers. Line 11 is supplied from another witness (see source_issues).

thinai_evidence.note: the man's planned journey for wealth, overheard in his sleep

25.reading: The friend tells the man that he would cross the waste where fire rings a hill of dry bamboo with rutting elephants inside, as fire ringed the lac house built by the plot of the blind king's eldest son with the five kings within, and where the bull elephant, as the wind's son broke the lac house and went out with his kin, tramples a path through the smoke and leaves with his herd; let him hear her state: her eyes, flower-like while he is near, weep when he is a little away, like the bond of base men who praise to the face and slander behind; her bangles, firm while he loves her, slip when he goes, like the bond of those who eat a man's wealth and fail him in decline; her brow, bright when he praises her, pales when he does not, like the bond of mean men who tell a secret once parted; he knows all this better than they do: her beauty when his grace is withdrawn is like the world when the sky withholds its rain.
25.nuance: The opening retells the burning of the lac house from the Bharata story, with Bhima, the wind's son, breaking out with his kin; the elephant that leads its herd out of the fire is the hero of that simile, and the man is about to do the opposite. The three refrains make her eyes, bangles and brow behave like false friends, loyal only while he is near and betraying her state once he goes. The phrase for the Kauravas' father in lines 1 and 2 (வயக்குறு மண்டிலம் வடமொழிப் பெயர் பெற்ற முகத்தவன்) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the man about to cross the burning waste

comparisons.vehicle: கை புனை அரக்கு இல்லைக் கதழ் எரி சூழ்ந்தாங்குக்
comparisons.tenor: the forest fire ringing the bamboo hill with elephants inside

comparisons.vehicle: அரக்கு இல்லை வளிமகன் உடைத்துத் தன் உள்ளத்துக் கிளைகளோடு உயப் போகுவான் போல
comparisons.tenor: the elephant breaking out of the fire with its herd
the elephant's trunk, like a door-bar
her eyes while he is with her

comparisons.vehicle: புறக்கொடையே பழி தூற்றும் புல்லியார் தொடர்பு போல்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes, bright while he is near and weeping when he goes

comparisons.vehicle: ஒல்கு இடத்து உலப்பு இலா உணர்வு இலார் தொடர்பு போல்
comparisons.tenor: her bangles, firm while he loves her and slipping when he leaves

comparisons.vehicle: பிரிந்தக்கால் பிறர்க்கு உரைக்கும் பீடு இலார் தொடர்பு போல்
comparisons.tenor: her brow, which pales and tells her secret when he is gone

comparisons.vehicle: வானம் துளி மாறு பொழுதின் இவ் உலகம் போலும்
comparisons.tenor: her beauty when his grace is withdrawn

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant guards its herd and tramples a path through the burning bamboo so that they go out together
iraicchi.sense: even the beast in the fire takes its own out with it, while the man would cross that land leaving his wife behind

26.reading: The friend recalls the woman's lament: spring has come to pain her, the kadamba in clusters like the god of the single earring, the seruntti in bud like the sun, the kaanji loud with bees like the fish-bannered god, the gnaazhal bright like the other god, the silk-cotton like the bull-bannered god, so that the bank is lovely like the five together; in this season when bees drink new honey, will he think of her shoulders that have lost their beauty; he who guards unfailingly those who come weary to his shade and is praised by the world lives in a stranger's land; will he pity the fading of her beauty at the holy Marudam ford, the change of her brow; and she tells her not to fret: the true word of their lover, with fighting elephants and victorious in battle, has come by messenger that he will come.
26.nuance: Each flowering tree is matched to a god by colour: the white kadamba to the one-earringed god, the seruntti to the sun, the kaanji to Kama of the fish banner, the gnaazhal to the other (probably the dark god), the red silk-cotton to Shiva of the bull banner. The refrain sets the man's public virtue, shelter to all who come to his shade, against his neglect of the one at home.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman pining in spring while the man is in a far land

comparisons.tenor: the bank adorned by the five trees together

27.reading: The friend tells the woman that spring has encamped like an enemy army in the land of an unworthy king whose foolish minister lets it in, with the riverbank trees flourishing like the wealth of a man who gives without stint and walks in virtue, mouval buds opening like women's smiles and the cool sand-stream streaked with pollen like the loosened hair of women joined with their lovers; she recalls the woman's laments (has he forgotten us while the cuckoo mocks and our beauty fades; does he not remember Koodal and its jewelled women; nor the play on the hill of the victorious spear-god who killed the sea-mango; nor the high sandbanks of the Vaigai where girls play) and tells her not to grieve with her pained heart: thinking she would be lost in loneliness, in the trembling season, at Kama's festival, their beloved drove his chariot fast and has come to her.
27.nuance: The similes are drawn from statecraft: spring is an enemy army let in by a foolish minister, and the trees thrive like a just giver's wealth; the season attacks the woman as a foe attacks a badly ruled land. The places of Madurai (Koodal, the spear-god's hill, the Vaigai) make the man's absence a loss of the city's shared pleasures.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman left behind in spring fears he has forgotten

comparisons.vehicle: அறன் அறிந்து ஒழுகிய தீது இலான் செல்வம் போல்

comparisons.tenor: the sand-stream strewn with pollen and leaves

comparisons.vehicle: பீடு இலா அரசன் நாட்டு, ஏதிலான் படை போல
comparisons.tenor: spring settling in, an invader in an undefended land

28.reading: When boughs and pools give their flowers as if unasked, garlands hang to the wearers' ears and the Vaigai's long clear stream parts the red sand like the hair of the lady of the lotus hung with ornament, the woman complains that if the flowers bloom, the cuckoo calls and he does not remember, he cannot think whether she can bear her grief, and what pity is that, as pallor creeps over her brow and her eyes lose their flower-beauty; the answer comes: do not speak so, there is no need to send the far one a message; he can bear separation no better than they; why grieve, he will come quickly.
28.nuance: The three refrains end in அளி என்னோ ('what kind of grace is this?'), a complaint against his lack of pity. Who answers in lines 21 to 24 is not marked: if the friend, it is the usual consolation; if the woman herself, she refuses to send a messenger and trusts that he suffers as much as she does, the stronger reading. Hence two speech situations.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman pining in the season while the man is away

comparisons.tenor: boughs and pools offering their flowers unasked
the Vaigai's streams parting the red sand

29.reading: When spring has come, the wide earth that gave many goods shedding its spent look and taking fresh beauty like a mother lying weak after childbirth, the long sand rippled like girls' play-sand, the stream parting the sandbanks like young girls' braided hair, pollen on the mango shoots like the spots on a dark girl's skin, the woman asks her friend whether she can hold back her heart, gone to the far one, beyond what the friend says, when the north wind touching the dewy flowers torments her; whether she can hide her state, when the evening with the dragonfly's lute-like hum torments her; whether she can be firm, when the scent of night-opened flowers torments her at night; and the friend answers that the one who removes their grief has come, not looking back to the wealth that bound him, drawn by her sweet speech.
29.nuance: The three torments run through the day: the north wind by day, the evening's hum, the night scent; the woman's three questions (can I hold, can I hide, can I be firm) answer the friend's counsel of restraint. Lines 10 to 21 are hers, the closing lines the friend's.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman whose heart has gone after the far-off man in spring

comparisons.tenor: the earth after the rains, spent and then renewed
the long sand marked with ripples

30.reading: In spring, when bees and dark dragonflies settle on boughs flowering like the joys of those who have done hard penance, the woman asks whether he would stay forgetting, bathing in the stream with peacock-like women while she swims sleepless, if someone told him 'the cuckoos are calling in the cool grove the sun never reaches'; whether he would forget among doe-eyed women at midnight if someone told him 'the bees hum in the budding jasmine of glorious Koodal'; whether he would play with bright-jewelled women at the high one's festival if someone announced 'the Vaigai runs round the flowering islet'; and the friend tells the man to make ready his tall chariot, for she, worn by unending sickness, trembles more than his famed enemies who would not bow at his feet.
30.nuance: The refrain is conditional (மன்னோ ... உளர் ஆயின்): he would not stay forgetting if only someone told him the season had come, so the blame falls on the missing messenger more than on him. The closing simile flatters the warrior (his enemies tremble) while making the woman's fear greater than theirs. The festival of உயர்ந்தவன் is a spring feast at Madurai; the god is not named.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman in spring fearing the absent man has forgotten

comparisons.tenor: the bees feasting in the flowering boughs
the women he may be playing with, peacock-like in bearing
her trembling, greater than that of his enemies

31.reading: The friend says that in this season, when the flood has cleared and the long pools are lovely, withered ingai flowers drop as if drawing lines on the sand, the beer flowers are pale like the brows of women parted from their lovers and the ponds bloom like the faces of the united, the cold dew and north wind come to confound them, beyond his vow that he would not lie; will this north wind, coming as the grain ears fill with milk, let them see him come in splendour on his elephant, having won the confused battle and seized land; will this light rain that blows on the bamboo blossoms let them see him come on his fine horse, sword victorious; will this hard dew let them see him come on his chariot with tribute; and she tells her not to be anxious: not failing the day he set, thinking she would suffer, the warriors with fierce spears have entered, as the tall flags of Koodal rise.
31.nuance: The season here is the cold of dew and north wind with ripening grain, not spring, and the man is away at war, not after wealth; his promised return from conquest at a set time is the mullai situation, but the woman's distress keeps the poem in separation. The three questions (விடுவதோ) fear that the season will kill her before she can see his triumph.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman waiting through the season for the man away at war

comparisons.tenor: the withered ingai flowers falling and lining the sand
the grain ears filling with milk

32.reading: The woman tells her friend that spring has come, its red sand gleaming like comb-parted dark hair, vengai blossoms spread like a gold garland set in braided hair, tender leaves dripping like the spots on a new mother, boughs not yet blossoming like the restraint of the wise who spread no talk, bushes humming with bees like a master's lute, branches swaying like good women dancing, trees heavy with clusters like the giving of the discerning and creepers twined like lovers' embrace; spring is good to those in love, she says, but not to her; yet now their lover has sent word, a medicine for her life against the pallor, that he comes for the fragrant jasmine by the cool falls, buds like her teeth; the message has come with words that end grief, so let them prepare the feast.
32.nuance: Line 8 plays on அலர், blossom and gossip: the boughs that have not yet burst into flower are like the restrained who do not spread talk, so the season keeps the lovers' secret. The eight similes of lines 7 to 12 all draw on human virtue or love. The message in lines 14 to 17 is hard to construe; this reading takes the jasmine 'like her teeth' as the season he names for his return.

thinai_evidence.note: word comes from the absent man in spring

comparisons.tenor: the red sand, gleaming and spotless
the vengai blossoms strewn on the sand
boughs whose buds have not yet burst open

33.reading: Spring has come, the pools swelling as if the rivers had opened their eyes to see the world's beauty, murukku petals scattering like coral on a gem-clear pool, buds opening like gems on every tree, and those joined with lovers do not loosen their embrace; but he who left her flower-like eyes lonely does not come; the silk-cotton flowers like fire, the punku drops petals like puffed rice, the kongam sheds pollen like gold; the season roars as if to mock the lonely, pallor covers her beauty, the boughs flourish as if laughing at her pain, her heart melts, the peacocks dance as if in scorn, her bangles slip, the streams run like her tears, and still he does not come or send word while bees hum like a flute holding the lute's note and the cuckoo calls; the friend tells her not to quarrel with the cuckoo or with him: not failing the day he set, the broad-chested man with his garland has come swiftly, driving his wind-fast chariot.
33.nuance: The middle of the poem is a run of 'as if' clauses (போலும்) in which the whole season seems to act against her: it roars, mocks, laughs and dances in scorn; her own body answers each one (pallor, melting heart, slipping bangles, tears). The return line (நாள் வரை நிறுத்துத் தாம் சொல்லிய பொய் அன்ற) repeats poem 31 almost word for word.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman abandoned to spring while the man stays away

comparisons.tenor: the pools swelling with new water

comparisons.vehicle: மணி புரை வயங்கலுள் துப்பு எறிந்தவை போலப்
comparisons.tenor: murukku petals on the clear pool
the boughs flourishing as if mocking her

comparisons.vehicle: என் கண் போல் இகுபு அறல் வாரும்
comparisons.tenor: the season's streams, running like her tears

comparisons.vehicle: நரம்பின் தீம் குரல் நிறுக்கும் குழல் போல்
comparisons.tenor: the humming of bees and dragonflies

34.reading: As the wide river, which in flood spread over the land and fed the world for the good of all living things, now runs lovely in thin streams, like men of worth who, having served one end first, turn at the last to serve another, spring has come with flowers falling and bees humming; the woman says she would hide the wrong of the man who did not fear parting, though the cuckoo calls bathed in kaanji pollen, but what can she do if her heart, withered like a tree under which a false witness sat, burns as if set on fire; if her eyes stream like the subjects under a king whose justice has failed; if her shoulders shrink and shed their bangles like the prosperity of one who lives on while his kin are ruined; and the friend tells her not to fret over her inner pain: not passing the day they counted, their lover has come with his trained horses, as a hand clears what troubles the eye.
34.nuance: All three refrain similes are moral and political: the tree that withers where a false witness sat (a belief also known from later texts), the people under a king who has failed in justice, and the wealth of one who thrives while his kin perish; her body's decline is a judgement on his conduct. The sense of the opening simile in lines 4 and 5 (men who serve one end and then another) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman bearing spring while the man who left is away

comparisons.vehicle: முன் ஒன்று தமக்கு ஆற்றி, முயன்றவர் இறுதிக் கண் பின் ஒன்று பெயர்த்து ஆற்றும் பீடு உடையாளர் போல்
comparisons.tenor: the river that fed the land in flood and still runs in thin streams

comparisons.vehicle: கரி பொய்த்தான் கீழ் இருந்த மரம் போலக்
முறை தளர்ந்த மன்னவன் கீழ்க் குடி போலக்

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, wasting and shedding bangles
his timely return ending her grief

35.reading: The friend tells the woman, as the trees flourish like the wealth of a man free of sloth, bees swarm in the boughs like those who share that wealth, tender leaves come like a dark girl's skin and pollen falls on them like the spots on that skin, not to sulk, looking at the mocking cuckoo with a breaking heart, that he has forgotten them: is this not the time, when bees drink the jasmine pollen by the cool falls on the Vaigai's high sandbanks, that he named when they sent him off in tears; the time of the bowman god's festival among the islands of the river; the time when the people of Koodal of tall mansions savour the new words born on the tongues of poets; and now, to ease the sickness that breaks her each time she remembers, the faultless lover, lord of the hill, has come on his bird-swift chariot with a day as true as truth.
35.nuance: The third season-sign is a literary one: the people of Madurai savouring new words born on poets' tongues (புலன் நாவில் பிறந்த சொல்), a picture of the city as a place of poetry. The returning man is called பொருப்பன், lord of the hill, a kurinji title in a paalai poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman fears the absent man has forgotten his promised return

comparisons.tenor: the day of his return, kept as truth is kept

36.reading: Peacocks dance around the high kadamba like the garland of the plough-armed god, bees hum like tuned strings, dragonflies like a bangled girl singing, honey-bees drone 'im' everywhere as if tuning, the trees blossom as if calling from place to place, the cuckoos call and the lovely season has come to welcome the festival of young spring; but, the woman tells her friend, their lover does not come: her brow is pale, her shoulders shrink, her eyes run hot like the season's streams, her heart burns between her breasts longing for the one who went through the hills; did he leave for love, did he forget with a single message, will they see his love, will he stay there; and her heart sighs like the smoke of the sacrifice that learned brahmins tend, remembering his saying that a long distance might come between them and mar her hair's beauty.
36.nuance: Unlike the poems before it, this one ends with no return: four questions (did he leave, did he forget, will we see, will he stay) and a sigh. The closing simile of sacrificial smoke and the words in lines 22 to 24 are hard to place: this reading takes them as the man's own parting words that she recalls.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman pining in spring for the man who has not come

links.note: In 13 the man tells the woman that if she came the stones would blacken her lotus soles, the beasts' cries would startle her and the hot wind would wither her; in 20 the woman takes the same objections (her feet, no water, no shade, the heat) and denies that any of them weighs against going with him.
links.teaches: Held together the two poems stage both sides of one dispute: the man argues from her body's frailty, the woman from her life's shortness and the deer pair that cross together, so the paalaikkali treats the wife's right to share the road as a question it argues, not a given.

links.note: In Akananuru 133 the man once asked the woman whether she could come with him, then crossed alone the forest where the twisted-horned stag keeps his young doe; in Kalittokai 20 the woman asks to go and the man refuses, saying the forest is too hot, while she points to the stag and doe that go together.
links.teaches: The two poems give opposite men, one who invites idly and one who forbids, while the deer pair on the road answers both: whoever speaks, the creatures of the waste show the journey can be shared, so the stag and doe work as the paalai poets' standing proof against the lone journey.

links.note: The friend argues that wealth moves from one to another by former deeds (பழ வினை), so leaving to earn it is pointless; Kural 619 holds that even when fate denies, effort pays the wage of the body's labour.
links.teaches: The friend uses the doctrine of former deeds to keep the man home, while the Kural grants that doctrine only to deny that it excuses idleness, so the same belief about fate served the akam poets as an argument against striving and the moralist as one to be overruled.

links.note: In both the friend (for one Kural commentator) tells the man who announces his going that the woman will not survive him: 'tell your quick return to those who will be alive' and 'she will not live a blink without you'.
links.teaches: The couplet's bare refusal of comfort becomes in the kali an argued case: the friend first sets his two promises against each other and shows that wealth cannot be earned, and only then says the girl will not live, so the Kural's line reads as the last move of a dispute the long poem spells out.

links.note: Naladiyar 45 scorns men who praise teeth as jasmine buds, having seen fallen teeth in the burning ground; in Kalittokai 22 the woman asks the man who praised her teeth like jasmine buds whether he praised them falling out.
links.teaches: Both deflate the same compliment with the same decay, but to opposite ends: the ascetic uses the fallen teeth to free a man from desire, the wife uses them to bind him to her for life, so the image of the body's ruin cut both for and against staying with a woman.

links.note: In 14 the woman says his past praise of her shoulders, eyes, teeth, brow, hair and breasts has turned to estrangement; in 22 she asks whether he has praised the same teeth, hair and breasts as they will be when old.
links.teaches: The two poems run the same catalogue of praise through time: 14 looks back at praise already withdrawn, 22 looks ahead to the aged body, so together they make the lover's blazon a promise that covers the whole life of the body, which leaving for wealth would break.

links.note: In both the woman tells her friend, before the man leaves, that she cannot survive his going: Kural 1155 asks her to stop it since union will be impossible once he goes, and Kalittokai 24 says her life has already gone with him.
links.teaches: The kali adds how she knows and why she yields: she learned of the journey from his sleep-talk and gives up her life to save his name from blame, so the couplet's plea to prevent the departure is shown coming from a woman who has already lost the chance to plead.

links.note: Kural 557: as the lack of rain is to the earth, so the king's lack of grace (அளி) is to those who live; Kalittokai 25: as is this world when the sky withholds rain, so is her beauty when his grace (அளி) is withdrawn.
links.teaches: The kali poet takes the moralist's image of rain and royal grace and applies it to a husband, so the man stands to his wife as a king to his realm and his leaving becomes a failure of rule, not only of love.

links.note: Kural 820 warns against the bond of those who are friendly at home and slander in the assembly; Kalittokai 25 compares her eyes, which shine while he is near and weep when he goes, to the bond of mean men who praise to the face and slander behind.
links.teaches: The friend turns the moralist's type of false friend into a figure for the woman's own body, whose eyes, bangles and brow publish her state once he leaves, so the danger the Kural sees in other people becomes, in love, the betrayal of the self by its own signs.

links.note: Purananuru 22 praises the Chera on campaign abroad, under whose white umbrella's shade the unarmed sleep safe while he does not sleep; Kalittokai 26 has the woman say her man guards unfailingly those who come weary to his shade, praised by the world, while he lives in a stranger's land.
links.teaches: The akam woman quotes the very virtue the puram poet praises, shelter given abroad to all who seek it, and asks why it does not reach her, so the pairing shows the cost of the heroic ideal falling on the household the hero leaves.

links.note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the generous man to a fruit tree ripening in the town; Kalittokai 27 likens the riverbank trees flourishing in spring to the wealth of a man who gives without stint and lives by virtue.
links.teaches: The comparison runs one way in the Kural (wealth like a tree) and the other in the kali (trees like wealth), showing that the moral image had become common enough for a love poet to turn it round and use the giver's wealth to describe the season.

links.note: Kural 639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm; Kalittokai 27 has spring encamp like an enemy army in the land of an unworthy king whose foolish minister let it in.
links.teaches: The Kural states the danger of a bad counsellor as a maxim, while the kali shows its outcome, the enemy camped inside the land, and uses that sight for spring's assault on a lonely woman, which shows the statecraft maxim already worked as a picture poets could borrow.

links.note: Kural 555: the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction wear away the wealth of the king who causes it; Kalittokai 34: her eyes stream like the subjects under a king whose justice has failed.
links.teaches: Read with the Kural, the woman's tears carry the threat the moralist gives to the subjects' tears, that they wear down the ruler who causes them, so her weeping is an accusation against the absent husband as well as a sign of grief.

links.note: Kural 788: friendship clears distress at once, as the hand of a man whose garment slips; Kalittokai 34: the lover has come on the promised day as a hand clears what troubles the eye.
links.teaches: Both use the hand that moves to the body without thought as the figure of help that needs no asking; the Kural gives it to friendship, the kali to a husband returning on the counted day, so the reflex image measures the ideal of timely help in both public and private bonds.
